note: First-pass dataset. Rarity tiers and regional ranges need review by a Kruger guide before launch — see docs/SPEC.md.

species.description: Pig-like body, tubular snout, donkey ears, arched back — but almost always after dark. Opens termite mounds with 20cm claws and laps up ants with a sticky tongue. A confirmed daytime sighting is one of Kruger's rarest events.
species.habitat: Woodland and grassland with termite mounds
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late on a night drive, well after dark

population.note: Not counted. Widespread across the park and almost never seen, so no survey has ever put a number on it.

species.description: Small striped hyena on stilt legs, mane raised along the spine when alarmed. Nocturnal termite specialist — laps up around 200,000 harvester termites in a single night. Rarely seen; night drives on open grassland give the best odds.

Nocturnal — dog-sized, hunched, dense black-and-cream spotting, black bandit mask. Trots along roads at night with head lowered. Never seen by day; night drives out of Olifants or Skukuza are your only real shot.

Grey giants with fan-shaped ears and heavy tusks — herds crossing the road, calves in the middle. Kruger holds around 20,000, one of the densest populations in Africa. Back off any bull that fans his ears and shakes his head.
species.habitat: Everywhere, concentrating near rivers in the dry season

species.description: Blotched brown, black and white coats — no two dogs alike. Packs sprint in a moving swarm, then collapse in a heap on cool tar. Around 250 left in Kruger, listed Endangered. Never follow at speed; sightings are prized.

Looks like a lean tabby with longer legs, upright ears and rich rufous behind the ears. Almost always nocturnal; the resident cat around Satara camp is the easiest bet. Interbreeds with feral cats — pure wild ones are getting scarce.
Troops of 15-30 charging across the road nose-to-tail, dark bands across a grizzled back. Constant twittering as they forage. Common throughout the park, often around Skukuza and Berg-en-Dal camps.

Silver-grey with a black face-mask and disc-like ears — small enough to fit in a hat. Very rare in Kruger, mainly on the central basalt plains around Satara. Lowers those ears to the ground to listen for termites underfoot.

Hook-lipped browser in thick bush, not the open plains — smaller than white rhino, ears rotating alertly. Just a few hundred left in Kruger after poaching. If it charges the car, stay in the vehicle and let it hit.

population.note: SANParks stopped publishing rhino numbers so that poachers cannot use them. Kruger holds one of the last significant populations left anywhere.

species.description: Fox-sized, russet flanks with a distinctive black saddle streaked silver. Trotting alone or in pairs at dawn and dusk; yipping howls carry across the veld after dark. Common throughout Kruger's open country.

Dark grey with a shaggy beard and forward-hooked horns, usually mixed with zebra on open plains. Central grasslands from Satara to Orpen are the stronghold. Nasal snorts carry a surprising distance in still air.

Shaggier and darker than spotted hyena, long mane over the shoulders, pointed ears. Extremely rare in Kruger — mostly the far north; scavenges alone at night. A daylight sighting is almost unheard of.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Deep night, far north — essentially chance

species.description: Chestnut-brown, faint white spots and stripes, straight spiral horns on the male only. Solitary in dense riverine bush — Letaba and Sabie forests are the easiest spots. Bounds off with a sharp dog-like bark.

Reddish-brown pig with a pale mane and pointed ear tufts. Nocturnal and secretive along dense riverine bush. No facial warts, no daytime trotting — a pig seen in the day is almost certainly a warthog, not this.

Massive black bulk, sweeping horns fused across the forehead in a heavy boss. Big herds churn watersides; solitary 'dagga boys' are unpredictable and cause more injuries than lions. Around 40,000 in Kruger.
species.habitat: Grassland and woodland near permanent water

species.description: Black-and-white banded quills up to 30cm long — rustling at night around camps. Africa's largest rodent. Never seen by day; try Skukuza and Olifants after dark. Quills detach on contact — they aren't fired.
species.habitat: Widespread; shelters in caves and burrows

species.description: Rufous cat with pointed black ear tufts, powerful hindquarters, no spots. Nocturnal and shy — seen from a car only a handful of times in a lifetime of visits. Can leap over 3m to swat a bird from mid-air.

Big dog-faced primate in troops of 30-plus, walking on all fours along the roadside. The 'wah-hoo' alarm bark warns of a leopard nearby. Keep windows shut — they raid vehicles and snatch food off laps.
species.habitat: Everywhere, especially near camps and koppies
species.bestTimeToSpot: Daylight — roosts in trees at night

species.description: Slim, small-headed cat with black tear-lines, spotted rather than rosetted. Usually on open plains, often on a termite mound. About 150 in the park, most between the Sabie and Crocodile rivers. Rarely near thick bush.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Mid-morning — hunts later than other cats

species.description: Small grey-brown antelope alone in the roadside grass — thin straight horns on the male, dark stripe down the muzzle. Bolts in a zig-zag rather than running straight. Present throughout Kruger but often overlooked.
species.habitat: Bush and woodland with good cover

species.description: Africa's largest antelope — huge cattle-like body, dewlap swinging under the throat, spiral horns on both sexes. Uncommon in Kruger; small herds mostly in the south. Knees make a distinct clicking sound as they walk.
Smallest African carnivore — russet-brown, size of a squirrel, standing sentry on a termite mound. Groups of 8-15, coordinated by high-pitched contact calls. Often nests inside disused termitaria.

Tiny rufous-grey mammal with a long trunk-like nose, darting between boulders on rocky koppies. Usually just a blur across a rock ledge. One of Africa's 'Small Five'; closer to elephants and aardvarks than to true shrews.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on rocks, before the heat

species.description: Head above the acacias, legs and neck out of proportion — usually silent, chewing at 5m up. Kruger holds several thousand and they browse over 60 tree species. Bulls stand with tails drooped; cows tuck into a canopy.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — visible from a distance

species.description: Grey-brown with vertical white stripes; bulls carry corkscrew horns close to 2m along the curl. Bounds across the road with tail flared white. Wooded thickets throughout Kruger; commoner than the size suggests.

Armour-plated body, bipedal walk with tail dragged, curls into a scaled ball when alarmed. The world's most trafficked mammal. A daytime road sighting is a once-a-decade Kruger event; report it to a ranger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Night drives — a handful of sightings a year

population.note: Never counted — there is no survey that finds them. The honest answer is that nobody knows, and that guides work here for years without seeing one.

species.description: Massive shapes half-submerged in permanent pools — Sunset Dam, Olifants, Sabie. Only eyes, ears and nostrils show by day; grazing on land at night. Kills more people than any other African mammal. Never block a hippo's path to water.

Low, stocky body, jet-black underneath with a bold silver-white saddle. Trots along at dawn and dusk ignoring almost everything. Tackles snakes, hives and even young lions — the reputation for fearlessness is earned.
species.habitat: Widespread; mostly nocturnal but active at dusk

species.description: Kruger's most abundant antelope, over 100,000 head — russet coat, black 'M' below the tail, lyre-shaped horns on the male. Explosive high leaps when spooked. Rutting males roar like a small lion through autumn.
species.habitat: Open woodland and the edges of riverine bush
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time of day, year round

species.description: Small rock-antelope on tiptoes, standing motionless on a boulder along the Lebombo hills or a rocky koppie. Fur is hollow-tipped and springs back — dries fast after rain. Pairs mate for life.

Nocturnal — slender, cat-shaped, long ringed tail, big rosetted spots. Comes into camps like Skukuza and Letaba for scraps; look for eyeshine along the fence at night. Not a cat at all — related to civets.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark in camp, or on night drives

species.description: Rosetted coat draped along a low branch, thick tail hanging. Most active dusk to dawn in riverine bush along the Sabie, Sand and Timbavati. Around 1,000 in the park; more common than sightings suggest. Look up when scanning trees.
species.habitat: Riverine bush, drainage lines and rocky ground
species.bestTimeToSpot: First and last light, on riverine roads

species.description: Never seen by day — golden torch-eyes reflecting, then a leap of 4m through the canopy. Baby-like wailing calls after dark are diagnostic. Common in acacia woodland; try the trees at camp fences after nightfall.
Straw-coloured cats sprawled in shade, or a pride crossing at first light. Distant roars carry 8km before dawn. Around 1,600 in Kruger; best odds on central plains around Satara and along the Sabie.
species.habitat: Open woodland and grassland near prey concentrations

species.description: Small grey-fawn antelope on rocky slopes — short forward-curving horns on the male, black scent-gland patch below the ear. Very few in Kruger; try the ridges above Berg-en-Dal. Sharp whistle when startled, then bounds off.

Rusty-slate males with white leg-stripes and lyre-tipped horns; females look like a different species — bright chestnut, unhorned, boldly striped. Dense riverine bush in the north — Letaba and Pafuri. Herd looks like two different animals.
Black-and-white striped horses in mixed herds with wildebeest — no two zebra share a stripe pattern. Loud yelping bark when alarmed. Common on central plains from Satara to Lower Sabie.

Big, red-tan antelope with a black-and-white face-mask and scimitar horns; both sexes horned. Fewer than 100 remain in Kruger — try the far north around Shingwedzi. Second-largest African antelope after eland.

Bulls jet-black with white belly and long scimitar horns swept back over the shoulders; cows chestnut. Small herds around Pretoriuskop and the western mopaneveld near Phalaborwa. Around 500 in the park — uncommon and localised.

Bounds across the road at night, long black-tipped ears, white belly flashing. Common everywhere but crepuscular — dawn, dusk and night drives. Sits tight until you nearly stand on it, then breaks with a big zig-zag.

Long-legged spotted cat with huge upright ears, roughly Labrador height — much taller than caracal. Very rare from a car; try wet grasslands around Nsemani Dam and Satara. Leaps to pounce on rodents through grass by ear alone.
species.habitat: Tall grass and reedbeds near water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dawn and dusk in marshy areas

species.description: Small rufous-brown antelope speckled with white hairs on the back, hunched rump. Only in dense bush in the north — Shingwedzi and Punda Maria. Male has tiny straight horns; female none. Solitary and nocturnal.
Rich rust-brown, long body low to the ground, tail with a black tip held up like a flag when running. Solitary. Bolts across the road with an unmistakable straight tail-flick.

Sandy-fawn antelope in tall reeds and grass near water; males have short forward-curving horns and a dark facial stripe. Small population around Mopani and Shingwedzi. High-pitched whistle when alarmed, then a bounding retreat.
species.habitat: Tall grass and reedbeds near water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dawn and dusk in wetland areas

species.description: Barrel body, sloped back, dark spots on tan flanks, head lowered as it trots. Whooping calls at night are diagnostic. Clans of 20-plus around den sites, often under road culverts. Around 2,000 in Kruger — commoner than lion.
species.habitat: Widespread; dens in culverts and drainage lines
species.bestTimeToSpot: Just after gate opening or before closing

species.description: Small rusty antelope, upright ears out of proportion, no belly stripe. Male has straight vertical horns; female none. Bolts a short way then freezes and looks back. Common in open country throughout the park.

Tiniest antelope in Kruger — reddish-brown, back speckled with white, tail whipping side to side when moving. Only in the Pafuri sand forest in the far north. Nocturnal and near-invisible; a daytime sighting is genuinely exceptional.
species.habitat: Dense sand forest and thicket in the far north

species.description: Larger than lesser bushbaby, silver-grey with a bushy tail longer than the body. Piercing 'crying baby' scream at night around northern camps — Letaba, Punda Maria. Torch-eyes reflect a deep amber.
species.habitat: Riverine forest, especially in the north

species.description: Small grey-brown squirrel flicking its tail on an acacia branch, chattering an alarm at everything. All over the park — often the first thing you hear at camp. Called the 'bushveld sentinel' for good reason.

Dark chestnut with a sloping back and glossy purple-blue patches on the thigh and shoulder. Africa's fastest antelope, capable of over 80km/h. Around 200 in the park; northern basalt plains near Mopani. Often up on a termite mound.
Silver-grey with a black face and white brow; males show an unmistakable turquoise-blue scrotum. Troops around picnic sites and camps will grab food from a car window. Common throughout the park.

Grey with wart-like facial pads, tail held straight up like an antenna when trotting off. Often kneels to feed on grass roots — the calluses on the wrists are permanent. Common in open country everywhere.
species.habitat: Open grassland and around rest camps

species.description: Shaggy grey-brown with a bright white 'toilet-seat' ring on the rump — impossible to miss. Bulls carry heavy, ridged, forward-curving horns. Always within a kilometre of water; try Letaba and Olifants riverbanks.
species.habitat: Riverine grassland within a few kilometres of water

species.description: Wide square lip and a heavy shoulder hump for grazing, calf usually walking ahead of the mother. Numbers collapsed under poaching — around 2,000 left in the park, down from over 10,000 in 2010.

population.note: SANParks stopped publishing rhino numbers so that poachers cannot use them. What is public is the direction: sharply down.

species.description: Nocturnal, long-legged, dog-sized mongoose with a striking bushy white tail. Trots along roads in headlight beams. Largest African mongoose. Almost never seen by day; best on night drives from Skukuza, Satara or Olifants.
Swims with only a kinked neck above the surface, which is how it got the name snakebird. Spears fish rather than grabbing them, then sits with its wings spread to dry.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Midday, wings out on a dead branch

species.description: Snow-white head and chest over chestnut and black, and the ringing call thrown back over its shoulder is the sound most people associate with African water, whether or not they know the bird.
Dark grey and slimmer than the other hornbills, with a bill like a scythe. Flies in a deep swooping bound and whistles a plaintive, rising *phee-phee-phee*.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, calling from a bare branch

species.description: Black above, white below with heavy black streaks, and fast — it hunts francolin and guineafowl in a flat charge through the trees rather than a stoop from height.
Cinnamon, with a black-and-white barred back and a crest it raises like a fan when it lands. Probes the ground with a long curved bill. Named for the call, which is exactly hoop-hoop-hoop.
Chestnut, with a blue frontal shield and preposterous toes that let it walk across floating lilies as though on solid ground. The male carries the chicks tucked under his wings.
Glossy black, with a bill that does not close — the gap is a tool for holding water snails while it cuts them out of the shell. Nothing else in the park looks like it.
White, with red legs and a face like a mask, and a grey bill flattened into a spatula that it sweeps side to side through the water.
Black, with a chestnut back and a scarlet face, and almost no tail at all. Rocks side to side in flight like a tightrope walker, which is what the French name means.
species.habitat: Open savanna, hunting on the wing

species.description: The heron that hunts away from water — stalking mice and frogs across open grass, well away from any river, which surprises everybody the first time.
species.habitat: Open grassland, often nowhere near water

species.description: Black, white and grey in bold blocks, with a call like a hammer on an anvil — which is exactly where the name comes from. Nests on open ground and will dive at anything that comes near.
Plain chocolate brown with startling yellow eyes and bare legs — the bare legs are the point, because it hunts snakes and scales stop fangs. Sits bolt upright on a dead tree for hours.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Midday, perched on a dead tree

species.description: Heavy, skulking and copper-backed, with a black cap and a red eye. Its call is a descending bubble of notes that sounds like water pouring from a bottle, and it means rain is coming.
Every camp has them and everybody photographs them anyway. Looks black until the light catches it, then goes electric blue-green with a bright orange eye.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, on the table next to you

species.description: Bigger and creamier than the white-backed, with a bare blue throat patch and dark eyes. It breeds on cliffs outside the park and only visits, so one here is genuine luck.
species.habitat: Ranges widely; breeds on cliffs elsewhere
species.bestTimeToSpot: At a large carcass, among White-backed Vultures

species.description: The largest bird alive and the fastest thing on two legs. In Kruger it keeps to the open southern and central grasslands, so it is a sighting you drive to rather than one that finds you.
species.habitat: Open short grassland and sparse savanna

species.description: Sandy brown with a black cap ringed in white and long red legs. Lives on burnt ground and short grass well away from water, and screams at you for driving past.
species.habitat: Short grass and recently burnt veld

species.description: Not a goose but a shelduck, and the loudest thing at any waterhole. Pairs bond for life and will see off animals many times their size to defend a nest.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, at the water's edge

species.description: The plainer cousin of the lilac-breasted, and a long way from home — it breeds in Europe and spends our summer here. All-over turquoise with a cinnamon back, and no long tail streamers.
species.bestTimeToSpot: November to March only; a summer visitor

species.description: Glossy black with red eyes and a deeply forked tail. A gifted liar — it copies other animals' alarm calls to scare them off food and then takes it.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, on a fence or dead branch

species.description: Crow-sized, which is startling the first time — Africa's largest kingfisher, shaggy-crested, with a bill like a chisel. Usually heard clattering off downriver before it is seen.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning, low over the water

species.description: The largest heron on earth — nearly a metre and a half of rust-and-slate patience standing in the shallows. Once you have seen one, every other heron looks like a rehearsal.
species.habitat: Quiet backwaters of the big rivers and dams
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning, motionless at the water edge

species.description: Brilliant white and long-necked, with a yellow bill that turns black when it is breeding. The biggest of the white egrets and the most elegant thing at any dam.
Long-tailed, grey and permanently outraged. Its call is an unmistakable nasal *g'way*, which is why every hunter in the lowveld curses it — it announces you to everything within a kilometre.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, complaining from the top of a tree

species.description: Tall, grey and unhurried, with a black eyebrow running back from a yellow eye. Stands in the shallows for so long that people mistake it for a stick.
You will hear it long before you see it. An iridescent green wing-patch and a call like somebody dropping a saxophone down a stairwell, usually at 05:00.

All brown, with a heavy crest at the back of the head that gives it the hammer profile it is named for. Builds an enormous domed nest, big enough to hold a person, and Africa is full of stories about it.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon, hunting frogs in shallow water

species.description: Runs down the middle of the road ahead of the car rather than stepping aside, for miles, and never learns. Blue head, red cap, body like a spotted rugby ball.
The small, dark one at the edge of the scrum, waiting for the big vultures to finish. Thin bill for picking scraps the others cannot reach. Critically endangered and still overlooked.
species.bestTimeToSpot: At a kill, on the outside of the crowd

species.description: Among the heaviest flying birds on earth, and it walks the open grassland like it owns it. A displaying male inflates his throat into a startling white balloon.
The largest vulture in Africa and the one that opens the carcass: its bill gets through hide the others cannot. Bare pink head hung with heavy folds of skin.
species.habitat: Open savanna; nests in flat-topped trees

species.description: Lilac chest, turquoise belly, and the most photographed bird in the park by a distance. Named for the tumbling aerial roll the male throws himself into on display.
species.habitat: Open woodland, perched on dead branches and posts

species.description: Green above, deep gold below, with a black gorget and a turquoise eyebrow. Sits in pairs on a low stem, dashes out for a bee, and comes back to exactly the same twig.
Black and white with a tail longer than the rest of it. Sits in small noisy groups on the top of a thorn tree and drops onto insects in the grass.
Barely bigger than your thumb and impossibly bright — cobalt above, orange below, with a red dagger of a bill. Sits on a reed a hand's width above the water.
species.habitat: Reeded edges of dams and slow rivers
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, on a low reed at the water line

species.description: Enormous, bald and stooped, with a pink throat pouch that inflates as it displays. Genuinely ugly and genuinely magnificent, and it stands at a carcass among the vultures like an undertaker waiting to be paid.
species.habitat: Carcasses, rubbish pits and drying pans
species.bestTimeToSpot: Midday, at a kill or soaring on the thermals

species.description: Africa's largest eagle — dark hood, spotted white belly, powerful enough to take a young impala. Territories run to hundreds of square kilometres, so sightings are widely spaced.
species.habitat: Open savanna; perches on tall dead trees

species.description: A huge ginger owl that watches the water from a low branch, spots the ripple a fish makes, and drops on it. In Kruger it is essentially a Luvuvhu River bird, and the hardest of the Big Six.
species.habitat: Tall riverine forest along the Luvuvhu

species.description: Black and white, and the only kingfisher that hovers — it hangs dead still over the water, then folds and drops. Every causeway in the park has a pair.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, hovering over open water

species.description: Green and violet with a crimson flash in the wing that only shows in flight. The green is a real pigment rather than a trick of the light, which is rare in birds.
Builds the untidy stick tenements that hang off the western side of tall trees and windmills. Easy to see and almost never looked at, which is the joke of the Small Five.
species.habitat: Open woodland, usually near large trees and camps
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, around camps and picnic sites

species.description: Lives on the backs of buffalo, giraffe and rhino, eating ticks and reopening wounds. A yellow ring around a red eye, and a hiss that warns the whole herd you are there.
species.habitat: On the backs of large mammals
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time you find a buffalo herd

species.description: Individually forgettable, collectively the most numerous wild bird on earth. Flocks move like smoke and can strip a field in an afternoon.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon, coming to drink in thousands

species.description: Huge black-and-white stork with the diagnostic tricoloured bill: red, with a black band and a yellow 'saddle' at the base. Male has dark eye, female yellow. One of the 'Big Six'; around 20 breeding pairs in Kruger.

Grey eagle-like head on ridiculously long pale legs — walks 20-30km a day hunting snakes. Long central tail feathers, black quills fanned behind the head; IUCN Endangered. Central grasslands around Satara.
species.habitat: Open grassland and lightly wooded savanna
species.bestTimeToSpot: Walking open ground in the morning

species.description: All carmine-red body with a turquoise crown and rump. Rides on kori bustards and even ostriches to catch flushed insects. Intra-African migrant, arriving in Kruger around September and departing March.
species.bestTimeToSpot: September to March only; a summer visitor

species.description: Turkey-sized black bird walking through grass; adult has bright red face and throat — female shows a dab of purple-blue on the throat. World's largest hornbill; IUCN Vulnerable (Endangered in South Africa). Booming dawn call carries 3km.

Breeding male has bright yellow body with a black face-mask that stops at the throat, and a red eye — Village Weaver has a black-and-yellow back and darker mask. Weaves round nests hanging from thorn trees.
species.habitat: Camps, reedbeds, anywhere with a thorn tree
species.bestTimeToSpot: Spring and summer, weaving over water

species.description: Slim red bill (the whole bill red, not yellow), pale head, spotted black-and-white back — the red bill is the diagnostic against Southern Yellow-billed Hornbill. Common in acacia woodland throughout Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, low down beside the road

species.description: Bright yellow banana-shaped bill on a hornbill with a spotted black-and-white back and pale head — nicknamed 'flying banana'. Bounces along beside cars begging at picnic sites. Common everywhere in Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, usually at eye level beside the road

species.description: Variable pale-fawn to dark brown eagle, feathered legs, gape reaching under the eye — Brown Snake Eagle has bare pale legs and a big yellow eye. Common perched eagle in open Kruger country.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, soaring or on a kill

species.description: Small brown plover with a striking double black chest-band, white forehead and red eye-ring. Runs a few steps and stops on gravel edges of dams and rivers. Any low-water bridge in Kruger.
species.habitat: Muddy edges of dams and rivers
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, at the water line

species.description: Africa's largest owl — pale grey plumage, salmon-pink eyelids visible when it blinks — a diagnostic mark by torchlight. Deep grunting 'hunh-hunh' at night. Widespread but scattered throughout Kruger.
species.habitat: Large trees along rivers and drainage lines
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dusk, or roosting by day if you know the tree

species.description: Grey-brown wader with a big yellow eye and pale grey wing-bar — Spotted Thick-knee has spotted wings and prefers dry ground. Always near water; trilling whistles at dusk. Try Sabie and Olifants sandbanks.

Pale golden-buff bird with an unmistakable heart-shaped white face — no ear tufts. Silent flight; blood-curdling screech at night. Roosts in disused buildings; check camp workshops and thatched roofs.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark, low along the road edge

species.description: Most abundant vulture in Kruger — dark brown body with a bright white lower back visible in flight (Cape Vulture is much paler overall). Cluster on carcasses in noisy squabbles. IUCN Critically Endangered.
species.habitat: Open woodland; nests in tall trees
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late morning, circling or at a carcass

species.description: White forehead, black eye-mask, brilliant red throat, buff belly — Little Bee-eater has a yellow throat. Colonial nester in vertical riverbanks; try Olifants and Letaba cuttings. Resident year-round in Kruger.

The only Kruger vulture with a clean white head and a pink-orange bill; black-and-white body. Often first at a carcass — hunts as well as scavenges. IUCN Critically Endangered; few pairs left in Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late morning, first at a fresh carcass

species.description: Turquoise-and-blue kingfisher with a red upper bill and black lower — bright blue tail in flight. Piercing trilling call all day. Intra-African migrant, arriving mid-November and departing mid-March — the sound of Kruger summers.
species.bestTimeToSpot: November to March, calling from a bare branch

species.description: Glossy black stork with a fluffy white neck and belly — the 'wool' is diagnostic. Slow deliberate walk through wet ground and along rivers. Widespread but scattered in Kruger; often solitary.
White stork with a pink wash on the wings, red face and a slightly down-curved yellow bill. Wades in shallows sweeping the open bill from side to side. Try Sunset Dam and Lake Panic hide.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, in groups at the water

species.description: Slate-grey to olive rather than black — the inside of the mouth is jet-black, hence the name. Up to 3m and among the world's fastest snakes. Shelters in termite mounds and hollow trees. Untreated bites are almost always fatal.
species.habitat: Woodland, termite mounds and rocky ground
species.bestTimeToSpot: Warm mornings — observe from the vehicle only

species.description: Slim tree snake, males emerald green, females olive-brown, with an outsized eye. Draped motionless along a branch. Rear-fanged; venom is highly dangerous but slow-acting, and the snake is calm — bites are rare.

Domed shell blotched black on yellow — named after the cat. The largest tortoise in southern Africa and one of the 'Small Five'. Often ambling across the road; drive round it, never lift or move one. Easily lives 80 years.

Grey-brown with pink-and-black throat bands visible when hooded. Sprays venom over 2m into the eyes, aimed at anything moving. Common around camps at night. If it hoods up, back away — do not throw anything.

Log-shape at the water's edge — often only eyes and nostrils showing, or a whole 4m body on a sandbank at midday. Explosively fast into water. Common in every permanent river; Sabie and Olifants are the best.

Thick, sluggish body patterned in grey-brown chevrons, arrow-shaped head. Lies motionless on roads and paths — the reason it accounts for more African snake bites than any other. Never step off a road onto grass without looking.
species.habitat: Everywhere; often on warm roads at dusk
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon, on tar still holding the day’s heat

species.description: Africa's largest snake — up to 5m, patterned brown and cream, non-venomous. Kills by constriction and will take small antelope. Often crossing roads warmed by tar. Protected inside Kruger.
species.habitat: Riverine bush, rocky outcrops and dense cover

species.description: Big grey-black lizard up to 2m, forked tongue flicking, laterally flattened tail for swimming. Along rivers and dams — often at Sunset Dam. Swims well and climbs trees. Bite is nasty; keep clear.

Look for tiny funnel-shaped pits in soft sand under thatch and along paths in rest camps — the larva waits at the bottom. Drop a grain of sand in and the trap-jaws will flick. Adult resembles a small, dull dragonfly. One of Africa's 'Small Five'.
species.habitat: Fine dry sand under trees, out of the rain
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any picnic site — look down before you look up

species.description: Chunky black or dark-brown beetle, males with a curved horn on the head — one of Africa's 'Small Five'. Buzzes into camp lights at night, especially in summer. Sluggish and harmless; grip strength is astonishing for the size.
species.habitat: Woodland; larvae develop in rotting wood and dung
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer nights, at camp lights after rain

species.description: Massive smooth-barked trunk with stubby branches like roots pointed at the sky — the 'upside-down tree'. Only in the far north, from Punda Maria up to Pafuri. Some individuals over 1,000 years old; hollow trunks store thousands of litres of water.
species.habitat: Hot, dry country north of the Olifants
species.bestTimeToSpot: North of Mopani, impossible to miss

species.description: Tan coat with darker shoulders and lyre-shaped horns bent tight, often standing on a termite mound. Reintroduced to the far north around Punda Maria in the 1980s after local extinction. A sighting anywhere in Kruger is exceptional.
species.habitat: Open sandveld and grassy woodland in the far north
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on the Nwambiya sandveld, and mostly luck

species.description: Bare red throat and face, blackish bill and legs — Natal Spurfowl has an orange bill and no red throat. Male perches on a termite mound at dawn to give a rasping crow. Common in open bushveld.
species.habitat: Grassland, old lands and roadside verges
species.bestTimeToSpot: First hour of light, on the road edge

species.description: Mottled brown with a yellow-and-red bill and orange legs. The camp bird — scratches around Skukuza and Lower Sabie as if it pays rent.
species.habitat: Thicket, riverine bush and rest camps

species.description: Carries its tail cocked like a bantam, which no other francolin here does. The pale eyebrow stripe runs the length of the head.
Small lapwing with a plain brown body and only a small white forehead patch — much drabber than Blacksmith or Crowned. Very localised in Kruger — the north around Punda Maria on burnt grasslands.
species.habitat: Burnt grassland and bare short-grass plains

species.description: Black with a clean white breast and collar, and far too clever. Works the picnic sites and the gates, and will be waiting on the table before you have unpacked.
A long-necked bustard on tall grass plains. The male throws his head back and makes a sound like a cork being pulled, then a swallow.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer mornings, males calling from a rise

species.description: Small brown bustard with a raised red crest visible only in display. Male's dramatic aerial display: flies vertically 20m, folds wings, drops like a stone, pulls up at the last second. Common in dry bushveld.
Comes to water in flocks in the last light and is gone before dark. The male carries two neat bands across a white forehead.
species.bestTimeToSpot: The last half hour before gate closing

species.description: The biggest of the lapwings, with yellow face wattles and a streaked throat. Noisy on damp ground near rivers and pans.
species.habitat: Damp grassland beside rivers and pans

species.description: White body, bare black head and neck, and a heavy curved bill. Mummified by the ancient Egyptians in their hundreds of thousands — some catacombs hold millions of them.
Chestnut-and-black duck with a clean white face — nothing else in Kruger looks like it. High three-note whistle in flight, often at night. Big rafts on pans and dams; try Sunset Dam and Lake Panic.
species.habitat: Pans, dams and quiet river edges

species.description: All black with a yellow bill and startling red legs. Bolder than any other crake — walks out onto lily pads in the open.
species.habitat: Reeds and floating vegetation on quiet water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning at a dam wall

species.description: Grey, with a bare yellow face that flushes red when it is excited. Its legs bend both ways at the joint, which lets it reach into tree holes after nestlings.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Mid-morning, working along a tree line

species.description: Small black cormorant with a hooked bill and a long tail — African Darter has a straight dagger bill. Perches drying wings after diving. Common on every dam and permanent river in Kruger.
Black bill, black legs and bright yellow feet. Hunts by running about in the shallows and stirring the mud with those feet.
Small stocky white egret with a thick neck and short yellow bill — Little Egret is slim with a black bill. Follows buffalo and elephant to snap up flushed insects. Common throughout the park.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, wherever the herds are

species.description: The voice of a Kruger night: "Good Lord, deliver us." Sits on the warm tar after dark and shows two red eyes in the spotlight.
species.habitat: Woodland edges and the road itself
species.bestTimeToSpot: On a night drive, on the road surface

species.description: Tiny, and hunts in daylight. Two black false eyes on the back of its head fool whatever is creeping up behind it.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Late afternoon — often mobbed by small birds

species.description: A grey scrap of bark the size of a fist. Almost impossible to see and easy to hear: one soft frog-like "prrrup" every few seconds, all night, in every camp.
species.bestTimeToSpot: After dark, torch on the call

species.description: Big black-and-white hornbill with a huge grey casque on top of the bill and red face-skin. Nasal wailing 'wa-a-a' call from the treetops — sounds like a crying baby. Northern riverine forest only, especially Pafuri.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, in the big trees along a river

species.description: White underparts, chestnut crown and dark blue back — Barn Swallow has a dark throat. Two extremely thin 'wire' tail streamers on the male; perches on bridge railings. Common along Kruger rivers year-round.
Here from September to April, having flown from Europe to do it. Hunts low over the road in front of the car.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer afternoons, low over the road

species.description: Rufous head and heavily streaked underparts. Builds a mud nest with a tunnel entrance under bridges and camp eaves.
Thin, grey and scythe-winged, always near palms. Glues its eggs to a vertical palm frond and hangs on while incubating.
Bill yellow with a red tip, no eye-ring — Red-billed Oxpecker has an all-red bill with a yellow eye-ring. Pale rump patch; prefers buffalo and giraffe. Uncommon in Kruger, more likely in the north.
species.habitat: On buffalo and giraffe, mostly in the north
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — scan a buffalo herd

species.description: The male puffs the white feathers of his rump into a ball the size of the rest of him. A loud clicking "chick-weeu" from the canopy.
Glossy jet-black tit with a bright white wing-edge panel. Family parties acrobatically search branches for insects, with sharp 'chick-a-dee' calls. Common in mixed woodland throughout Kruger.
Named after its own call — "dee-dee-dee-deederik" — which runs all summer. Lays in weaver and bishop nests and leaves them to it.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer, calling from an exposed perch

species.description: Glossy green-black with a long white-tipped tail and a red curved bill. Moves in noisy family parties that all cackle at once.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time — you hear the party first

species.description: Scruffy grey-brown mousebird with a long tail and a shaggy crest — no red face patch, unlike Red-faced Mousebird. Bill dark above, pale below; untidy little parties bomb into fruiting trees. Common in camps.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time, in a fruiting bush

species.description: Grey mouse-like bird with a long tail, bright red face patch and red bill — Speckled Mousebird has a plain face and dark bill. Whistled 'zwee-wewitt' in fast direct flight. Common in fruiting trees.
Green with a dull brown head and a flash of yellow under the wing in flight. Screeches overhead in pairs, usually going somewhere in a hurry.
species.habitat: Woodland with big trees, near water

species.description: A kingfisher that mostly ignores fish. Sits on a low branch watching the ground and drops on grasshoppers and lizards.
species.habitat: Woodland and camp gardens, often away from water
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time, on a low perch

species.description: Arrives in summer in loose flocks that call constantly overhead — a liquid "prrup" you learn to look up for. Chestnut back, yellow throat, blue below.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer, hawking high over open ground

species.description: Bright green, and invisible in a fruiting fig until it moves. Hangs upside down to reach fruit and gets drunk on the fermenting ones.

Larger and darker than Cape Turtle Dove, with a bare red eye-ring on a red eye. Slow six-note call rendered as 'I-AM-a red-eyed dove'. Common in wooded areas throughout Kruger, particularly around camps.
The bird behind the sound of the whole bushveld: "work harder, work harder", from before sunrise until well after dark.
Small, pinkish, with a speckled bib and no collar. The soft bubbling call is the one people mistake for a distant laugh.
species.habitat: Camps, roadsides and dry open ground

species.description: Grey-and-white shrike with a wispy white crest, yellow-fleshed eye-wattle and a bright yellow eye. Chattering parties of 6-10 move through the canopy together, with whistled 'weep' contact calls. Common in mixed woodland.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, when the party comes past

species.description: Scarlet face inside a heavy black collar. A pair sit side by side and duet so precisely that it sounds like one bird.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, duetting from a bare branch

species.description: Yellow, red and speckled, like something assembled from spare parts. The call is a long unbroken trill that sounds like an alarm clock.
The Afrikaans name means ghost bird, for a mournful drawn-out "hoooop" from deep cover. A heavy hooked bill and a pale eye — it kills lizards and small birds.
Brilliant yellow with a clean black hood and a coral bill. The liquid whistled "pooodleoo" is one of the best sounds in the canopy.
Never alone and never quiet. The whole group works itself into a babbling chorus, then crashes off through the undergrowth together.
Yellow under the tail, dark peaked cap, and the first bird calling in every camp. Cheerful to the point of being a nuisance at breakfast.
Stands very upright on open ground, heavily spotted below, and runs in short bursts. Flicks its wings open between stops.
Orange bill, orange flanks and a white throat with black stripes. Turns leaf litter over in the shade at the edge of a camp.
A warbler with no tail to speak of — it looks like a bird that has been cut in half. Creeps along branches like a nuthatch.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, in a mixed bird party

species.description: Small warbler, grey head, olive back, bright yellow breast — no black throat bar (Bar-throated Apalis has one). Long fine tail flicked side to side. Common in mixed woodland canopies throughout Kruger.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, high in a thorn tree

species.description: The male trails a chestnut tail twice his own length through the shade of a riverine tree. A blue eye-ring and bill to match.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer mornings, low in the shade

species.description: The big long-tailed glossy starling, duller and more purple than the cape glossy, and much heavier on the wing.
species.bestTimeToSpot: All day, often on the ground

species.description: Slate-grey back, orange underparts, long orange tail, and a bold white eyebrow — the eyebrow is diagnostic against other robin-chats. Melodic dawn song with mimicry. Common in riverine bush around Skukuza and Letaba.
Black and white, walking the wet rocks below a bridge with its tail going the whole time. Tame around low-water crossings.
species.habitat: River edges, rocks and low-water crossings
species.bestTimeToSpot: Any time, at a river crossing

species.description: Breeding male black with a white wing-panel and a yellow shoulder — much smaller than Long-tailed Widowbird. Non-breeding male and female streaky brown. In tall grass and reedbeds throughout Kruger.

Breeding male yellow, black head extending over the whole face and throat, back spotted black-and-yellow — Southern Masked Weaver has a plain yellow back and smaller mask. Noisy colonies in riverine trees.
species.habitat: Trees over water, camps and rivers

species.description: Breeding male is startling scarlet-orange with a black face and belly, fluffing out in display over reedbeds. Non-breeding male and female drab streaky brown. Colonies in reed-fringed pans, widespread wherever wet vegetation persists.
species.habitat: Reedbeds and rank grass near water

species.description: Male has an iridescent metallic-green head and chest above a clean white belly, thin curved bill. Female drab olive with white belly. Common in flowering aloes and camp gardens throughout Kruger.

Male matt-black with a metallic green crown and throat and a brilliant scarlet chest — nothing else looks like it. Female drab olive-brown speckled below. Common in flowering aloes and camp gardens throughout Kruger.

Small yellow-and-olive canary — bright yellow underparts and eyebrow, black malar stripe curving down from the bill. Melodious warbling song from thorn trees. Common in mixed woodland and camp gardens.
Plain grey head (no black face-mask like House Sparrow), chestnut back, one thin white wing-bar. Common at picnic sites and camp lawns, hopping under tables. Whistled 'chirrup-chirrup' call.
Powder blue face, breast and tail on a fawn back. Feeds on bare ground in small parties and is the first thing at a camp bird bath.
Striped black-and-white head, chestnut back and a deep yellow breast. Feeds quietly on the road verge and is easy to drive past.

Slender, upright fawn antelope with black glands below the ear and thin straight horns on the male. Very rare in Kruger — a handful only, mostly grasslands near Pretoriuskop. Bounces off with stiff-legged 'stotting' when flushed.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Early morning on the Pretoriuskop grasslands, and mostly luck

species.description: Sleek dark-brown swimmer with a pale throat, usually in family groups along the Sabie, Olifants and Letaba rivers. Uses hands, not teeth, to grab crabs from under rocks. Check low-water bridges early in the morning.
species.bestTimeToSpot: First light at a low-water crossing, sitting very still

species.description: Emerald green and scarlet, and completely invisible — it sits dead still with its green back to you and a call so soft you assume it is further away than it is. The best bird sighting in the park.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Summer mornings in the Luvuvhu forest, listening for a low hoot

species.description: Dark grey with a black face and pale throat — distinct from the vervet's silver-grey and black face. Found only in the Pafuri and Punda Maria riverine forest. Loud booming male call carries from the treetops at dawn.
species.habitat: Tall riverine forest, Pafuri and the Luvuvhu
species.bestTimeToSpot: Morning, high in the trees — listen for the branches

species.description: Flat olive-brown shell, long neck tucked sideways not backwards. Basking on logs and rocks in seasonal pans and mud pools. When a pan dries it buries into cracked mud and waits, sometimes years, for the next rains.
species.habitat: Seasonal pans, dams and slow water
species.bestTimeToSpot: After summer rain, walking between pans

species.description: A small owl barred across the head and chest, where its pearl-spotted cousin is spotted. Hunts at dusk from a low perch and will call in broad daylight.
species.bestTimeToSpot: Dusk, along the Luvuvhu and Sabie rivers
